passage: Drama teacher's note, 20 November. Written by Thomas. When we cast the annual play, I mixed students from the hill colony and the river colony, who usually keep to their own corners. Noor, fifteen, from the river side, was cast opposite Kavin from the hill side. For two weeks they rehearsed stiffly and ate lunch apart. The talk on respecting each other that we held in October had changed nothing. Then, a week before opening, the lighting board failed. Noor knew how to rewire it from her father's electrical shop; Kavin knew the cue sheet by heart. They stayed back three evenings together, fixing and running cues. On opening night they bowed holding hands with the whole cast. This week I have seen their friends eating lunch at the same table. The shared job did what the talk could not.

qa.q: What failed a week before opening?
qa.a: The lighting board.

qa.q: What might Noor have felt during the first two weeks of stiff rehearsals?
qa.a: She likely felt awkward and guarded around Kavin, keeping to her own colony's side as usual.

qa.q: What turned the cast around, and why did it work where the October talk failed?
qa.a: The lighting board failing forced Noor and Kavin to rely on each other's skills, so shared effort built trust that talk alone had not.

qa.q: How does Thomas seem to see the October talk now?
qa.a: Thomas sees that it changed nothing, and that the shared job on the play did what the talk could not.

grounding: Teenagers from two neighbourhoods on a school play must depend on each other to fix a crisis, and shared effort turns them into one group where a talk had failed.

passage: Saturday. Robotics regional tomorrow. Six months ago I'd have laughed if someone said I'd spend a Saturday night at Kishore's house. He's from the old town, I'm from the new colonies, and our lot and his lot have never mixed. Mr Das put us on the same team because Kishore can solder anything and I can code. At first we argued about everything. Then the arm kept failing, and neither of us could fix it alone. His soldering, my code, three weekends. Tonight his mother made us poha, and we tested the arm on her kitchen floor. It picked up the cup! We both yelled. When school had that respect-each-other talk last year, I yawned through it. Tonight I didn't even think about any of that. We're just the team. - Ujjwal

qa.q: What did Kishore's mother make for them?
qa.a: Poha.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal feel when the arm picked up the cup?
qa.a: Ujjwal was thrilled; they both yelled with joy after three weekends of work.

qa.q: What choice by Mr Das set this friendship up, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Putting Kishore and Ujjwal on one team with skills each needed, so they had to depend on each other to make the arm work.

qa.q: How might Kishore see the old-town and new-colony divide after these months?
qa.a: For Kishore it may matter less too, since he now welcomes his teammate at home and shares the win.

grounding: Two teenagers from different parts of town on a robotics team depend on each other's skills, and shared work makes them one team where a talk had not.

passage:
Kodlipet and Hosur sat on opposite banks of the same river, and their families had argued over the water for as long as anyone remembered. At the district school the two groups ate lunch on opposite sides of the ground.
Then the science teacher put Rashmi, fifteen, from Kodlipet, and Indu, from Hosur, on one team for the river-testing project. They needed samples from both banks every morning for three weeks, or the project would fail.
The first week the two girls barely spoke, handing jars over the school gate. In the second, Indu's bus broke down, and Rashmi walked across the bridge in the rain to collect her samples. In the third, they sat arguing over graphs in Indu's grandmother's kitchen until nine.
At the fair, when the judge asked whose idea the upstream test was, they both said, "Ours." Last year's assembly talk on tolerance had changed nothing.

qa.q: For how long did they need samples from both banks?
qa.a: Every morning for three weeks.

qa.q: What does Rashmi walking across the bridge in the rain suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she now cared about Indu and their shared project more than the old village rivalry.

qa.q: Why did the river project change them more than the assembly talk?
qa.a: They depended on each other to succeed, so shared effort turned them into a team in a way that words alone had not.

qa.q: How might the two villages see the girls' answer 'Ours' at the fair?
qa.a: It might surprise them, showing that children from rival banks could share credit, which could soften the old argument.

grounding: Two teenagers from rival villages who depend on each other for a science project come to see each other as one team, more than a tolerance talk managed.

passage:
At the comprehensive in south London, the kids from the Glenmore estate and the kids from the houses up the hill had kept to separate stairwells for years. A visiting speaker had once given an assembly about respect. Nobody remembered it.
Then Ms Hart cast the spring play. Kofi, sixteen, from the estate, would run the lighting desk. Beatriz, from up the hill, had the lead. In the storm scene she had to hit her mark at the exact second he dropped the lights, or she would be speaking in the dark.
They rehearsed that one cue forty times. He learned she counted under her breath; she learned he tapped the desk twice before every change. On opening night the lights fell, she turned, and the hall gasped.
Afterwards Beatriz ran up to the lighting box. "We did it!" Kofi grinned. Nobody said "you lot" that night.

qa.q: What did Kofi run for the spring play?
qa.a: He ran the lighting desk.

qa.q: What does Beatriz running up shouting 'We did it!' show about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt proud and included, seeing the success as shared with Kofi, part of one team rather than a separate group.

qa.q: Why did the storm cue do more than the respect assembly?
qa.a: Rehearsing one cue forty times made them depend on each other and learn each other's habits, which built trust that a talk had not.

qa.q: How might other estate and hill kids see Kofi and Beatriz after opening night?
qa.a: They might notice the two celebrating together and start seeing the other side as possible teammates.

grounding: Teenagers from different neighbourhoods who depend on each other in a school play become one team through shared effort, more than a respect assembly did.
